title: Leadership, Well-Being, and the Power of the Natural World
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Makes the case that leaders should deliberately connect team members with nature, citing research that frequent contact with the natural world improves vitality, mental clarity, mood, and compassion while reducing stress and burnout. It argues that humans evolved in close connection with nature, so the desire is nearly universal. Good leaders hold meetings and off-sites near natural settings, reward people with outdoor experiences, and use biophilic design to bring plants, water imagery, and patios indoors. The practical prompt is to ask how much nature the team is actually exposed to, given that people spend over 90 percent of their time indoors.
points: Frequent exposure to nature is linked to energy, clarity, lower stress, and lower burnout in fast-paced organizations.
Leaders can build nature into the work itself through off-sites near natural wonders and outdoor rewards such as hiking or kayaking trips.
Biophilic design (living walls, rooftop terraces, patios) brings nature into indoor workplaces when the outdoors is not available.
The closing question, how much nature is your team exposed to, turns the research into a concrete leader audit.
quotes: Humans evolved in close connection to nature, and the desire to connect with the natural world exists in nearly everyone. Leaders and workplaces that create opportunities for team members to commune with nature help to energize their workforce and diminish the burnout commonly experienced by team members in fast-paced organizations.

Good leaders understand the power of nature and encourage team members to spend as much time outdoors as possible. They often hold meetings and off-sites in close proximity to natural wonders so that team members can avail themselves of nature between sessions.

They know that the more time people spend outdoors and in nature, the healthier they become psychologically. Contact with nature recharges people and promotes a sense of connection to the larger world.

The benefits are so enormous that many leaders bring the outdoors inside. In what is known as biophilic design, some enterprises work hard to bring natural elements indoors through rooftop terraces, living walls (where plants grow and spread down a surface), video screens depicting waterfalls and forests, and outdoor patios where people can congregate and enjoy the outdoor world between meetings.

Given that people spend more than 90 percent of their time indoors, the more leaders push people to the outdoors, the better. How much nature is your team exposed to? In the presence of nature, the human spirit is fed and nurtured.
